meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a coherent methodological contribution (hard attention with decoupled pre-computed alignment training for morphological inflection) with solid empirical results on low-resource CELEX but mixed results on SIGMORPHON. The core issue is confounded causal attribution: three factors (mechanism, training procedure, alignment quality) are introduced together, making it impossible to determine which drives the improvement. All specialist reviewers identify this as critical. The paper would be substantially strengthened by: (1) ablation study isolating hard attention mechanism from decoupled training (e.g., hard attention with joint learning, soft attention with pre-computed alignments); (2) statistical significance testing with 95% confidence intervals for all results; (3) alignment quality analysis and sensitivity study (e.g., performance with degraded alignments); (4) quantitative representation analysis (silhouette scores, mutual information, probing classifiers) instead of 2D visualization; (5) controlled morphological typology experiment. The paper's claims should be qualified: CELEX results are strong but single-language; SIGMORPHON results are mixed (hard underperforms overall); Wiktionary improvements are marginal. The novelty is incremental (hard attention mechanisms exist in prior work; main contribution is application to morphology with decoupled training). The paper makes meaningful contributions but overstates generality and lacks empirical rigor. Recommend: (a) major revisions addressing confounded causal attribution and statistical significance, or (b) conditional acceptance with clear acknowledgment of limitations and unresolved confounds.
meta_review.author_guidance: Reviewers identify several critical issues that should be addressed: (1) Confounded causal attribution: Your CELEX improvement could stem from hard attention mechanism, pre-computed alignment supervision, or decoupled training. Conduct ablation study with four conditions: hard+pre-computed (current), hard+joint, soft+pre-computed, soft+joint. This isolates mechanism from training procedure. (2) Statistical significance: Report 95% confidence intervals for all results using bootstrap resampling. Conduct paired significance tests (McNemar's test) comparing hard vs. soft attention. Your CELEX improvement (1.14 pp) and Wiktionary improvement (0.21 pp) may not be significant. (3) Alignment quality: Report accuracy of Sudoh et al. (2013) CRP model on CELEX and SIGMORPHON. Conduct sensitivity analysis: evaluate hard attention with degraded alignments (10%, 20%, 50% error injection). This validates the critical A1 assumption. (4) Representation analysis: Supplement 2D SVD visualization with quantitative metrics. Compute silhouette scores for character clustering. Measure mutual information between position and representation. Train probing classifiers to predict character identity and position. (5) Morphological typology: Design controlled experiment. Analyze alignment quality per language. Visualize soft attention weights to assess long-range dependency learning. Perform ablation varying morphological properties systematically. (6) Hyperparameter fairness: Provide supplementary material with full hyperparameter details (learning rate, hidden size, dropout, epochs, early stopping). Confirm equal tuning effort for hard and soft attention. (7) Generalization: Evaluate on additional low-resource morphological datasets in other languages. This validates the low-resource claim beyond German CELEX. (8) Claim qualification: Revise abstract and introduction to accurately reflect mixed SIGMORPHON results (hard underperforms soft overall; outperforms only on suffixing languages). Avoid overstating SOTA claims. (9) Best-derivation approximation: Analyze derivation ambiguity. Compare best-derivation vs. marginalized objectives on a subset. (10) Supplementary material: Provide code, hyperparameters, and implementation details for reproducibility.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This paper proposes a hard attention mechanism for morphological inflection generation that explicitly models nearly-monotonic character-level alignments, trained on pre-computed alignments from Sudoh et al. (2013). The core contributions are: (1) hard attention architecture with explicit step/write actions, (2) decoupled alignment learning using pre-computed alignments, and (3) empirical validation across three datasets (CELEX, Wiktionary, SIGMORPHON2016). The paper demonstrates strong low-resource performance on CELEX (89.44% vs. 88.3% LAT) but mixed results on SIGMORPHON (95.61% hard vs. 96.34% soft overall, with hard outperforming only on suffixing languages). Five specialist reviewers converge on critical methodological concerns: (i) confounded causal attribution—hard attention gains may stem from mechanism, pre-computed alignment supervision, or decoupled training, with no ablation study isolating these factors; (ii) absent statistical significance testing across all results, making marginal improvements (1–2 percentage points) uninterpretable; (iii) unquantified alignment quality dependency; (iv) unclear hyperparameter fairness; (v) post-hoc morphological typology explanation without controlled experimentation. The paper makes meaningful contributions to morphological inflection but overstates generality and lacks empirical rigor. Novelty is incremental: hard attention mechanisms exist in prior work (RNN Transducer, Neural Transducer); the main contribution is application to morphology with decoupled training.
strengths: Clear architectural innovation with explicit linguistic motivation: hard attention with step/write actions directly exploits the nearly-monotonic alignment structure of morphological inflection, providing interpretable control over pointer movement.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three datasets with varying training set sizes (CELEX 500, Wiktionary 360k, SIGMORPHON 12.8k), demonstrating robustness across low-, medium-, and large-resource regimes.

Strong low-resource performance on CELEX (89.44% vs. 88.3% LAT, 87.62% MED), with learning curves (Figure 2) showing clear generalization advantage on development set despite similar training-set fitting.

Insightful representational analysis (Section 5) comparing learned alignments and character encodings between hard and soft attention, revealing that both models learn monotonic alignments but encode positional information differently.

Practical simplification of training procedure via decoupled alignment learning: using pre-computed alignments enables straightforward cross-entropy loss training without forward-backward algorithm complexity.

Honest discussion of limitations: paper acknowledges mixed SIGMORPHON results (hard underperforms soft on non-suffixing languages) and provides linguistic explanation, demonstrating transparency about scope of contribution.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: This paper presents a coherent methodological contribution (hard attention with decoupled pre-computed alignment training for morphological inflection) with solid empirical results on low-resource CELEX but mixed results on SIGMORPHON. The core issue is confounded causal attribution: three factors (mechanism, training procedure, alignment quality) are introduced together, making it impossible to determine which drives the improvement. All specialist reviewers identify this as critical. The paper would be substantially strengthened by: (1) ablation study isolating hard attention mechanism from decoupled training (e.g., hard attention with joint learning, soft attention with pre-computed alignments); (2) statistical significance testing with 95% confidence intervals for all results; (3) alignment quality analysis and sensitivity study (e.g., performance with degraded alignments); (4) quantitative representation analysis (silhouette scores, mutual information, probing classifiers) instead of 2D visualization; (5) controlled morphological typology experiment. The paper's claims should be qualified: CELEX results are strong but single-language; SIGMORPHON results are mixed (hard underperforms overall); Wiktionary improvements are marginal. The novelty is incremental (hard attention mechanisms exist in prior work; main contribution is application to morphology with decoupled training). The paper makes meaningful contributions but overstates generality and lacks empirical rigor. Recommend: (a) major revisions addressing confounded causal attribution and statistical significance, or (b) conditional acceptance with clear acknowledgment of limitations and unresolved confounds.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Reviewers identify several critical issues that should be addressed: (1) Confounded causal attribution: Your CELEX improvement could stem from hard attention mechanism, pre-computed alignment supervision, or decoupled training. Conduct ablation study with four conditions: hard+pre-computed (current), hard+joint, soft+pre-computed, soft+joint. This isolates mechanism from training procedure. (2) Statistical significance: Report 95% confidence intervals for all results using bootstrap resampling. Conduct paired significance tests (McNemar's test) comparing hard vs. soft attention. Your CELEX improvement (1.14 pp) and Wiktionary improvement (0.21 pp) may not be significant. (3) Alignment quality: Report accuracy of Sudoh et al. (2013) CRP model on CELEX and SIGMORPHON. Conduct sensitivity analysis: evaluate hard attention with degraded alignments (10%, 20%, 50% error injection). This validates the critical A1 assumption. (4) Representation analysis: Supplement 2D SVD visualization with quantitative metrics. Compute silhouette scores for character clustering. Measure mutual information between position and representation. Train probing classifiers to predict character identity and position. (5) Morphological typology: Design controlled experiment. Analyze alignment quality per language. Visualize soft attention weights to assess long-range dependency learning. Perform ablation varying morphological properties systematically. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Content: The following recommendations come from the ACL policy on publication ethics. The reviewer has to read the paper fully and write the content and argument of the review by themselves, subject to the secondary reviewer policy described above, and it is not permitted to use generative assistance to create the first draft. This requirement extends to the meta-review, and the reviewer has to write any meaningful argumentation in the meta-review by themselves. Generative assistance should be used responsibly. For instance, it is reasonable to use writing assistance to paraphrase the review, e.g. to help reviewers who are not native speakers of English. It is also reasonable to use tools that help to check proofs. Neither reviewers nor editors should upload a submitted manuscript or any part of it into a non-privacy preserving generative tool as this may violate the authors’ confidentiality and intellectual property rights and, where the paper contains personally identifiable information, may breach data privacy rights. This confidentiality requirement extends to the peer review report, as it may contain confidential information about the manuscript and/or the authors. For this reason, neither reviewers nor editors may upload their peer review report into a non-privacy-preserving generative tool, even if it is just for the purpose of improving language and readability. The ACL publication ethics committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct.
